utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-84-T, the Prosecutor versus Ramush Haradinaj et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber was informed that Mr. Guy-Smith would, as matters stand now, would have no questions. The Chamber has decided that Mr. Emmerson gets the five minutes he asked for, and the Chamber understood that you, Mr. Harvey, will use approximately 15 to 20 minutes for cross-examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour. Mr. Crosland should be out of here in time for coffee.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Re's indicated on current form the re-examination of approximately a similar to Mr. Harvey so Your Honour has an idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Crosland, that gives you an impression of what you could expect for this morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Unless you are spoiling the schedule, which of course -- you just have to answer the question. If that takes two hours, Mr. Crosland, we accept that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We would like to hear your evidence; but before you give that evidence, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you gave on the 19th of April in this court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, I wonder if you could be kind enough to pull up P45 on the screen, and if Colonel Crosland could be given the green volume at behind tab 3. It is the same image.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You can see the image on the screen. If you need to look at the hard copy, it's mind tab 3. I'd like to ask you to make some markings on the screen, and if Madam Usher could assist you to make markings. In light of the answers you gave yesterday, I'm not going to ask you to mark the specific positions of the bodies you saw floating because you gave some descriptions and evidence about that in chief. Do you see the road -- the track that moves off from almost the middle of the picture to the right-hand side?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Is that the track by which you approached?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suspect it was, sir. The reason I'm hesitating is to try and orientate.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think if I can help you --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: We came -- I beg your pardon. We came in -- I think it probably was that track. I'm trying not to confuse it with the visit to the place with Lord Ashdown.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. I understand because you went there twice. Can I be clear one or two matters on this then. I won't ask you to mark that given that response. Do you see to the -- above on the photograph, above that track which I think would be south on the map, there are rows of bushes or what look like bushes?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, sir, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Was anything said to you by the Serb officials about having seen bodies in that area?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I can recall, sir, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Was anything said to you by the Serb officials about having found bodies, including the body of a woman and child, inside the farm buildings that you can see rather indistinctly in the top right-hand quadrant of that photograph?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall anything -- any information of that sort, no, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. That's all I need to ask you then about that photograph, and then I have one other topic to ask you about and it's this. You gave some evidence in the Limaj case, and we have your transcript, about the fact that from time to time bodies of civilians would be found, either by the side of the road or in various locations, in different parts of Kosovo. First of all, is that something which also occurred in the Dukagjini region from time to time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we did or we were asked to go and visit where bodies had been left by the side of the road. If I recall rightly, I think there was at least one instance outside of -- on the Pec-Pristina road closer very much closer to Pec, and I think maybe down at Rakovina, north, north-east of Djakovica was another occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I just want, if I may, to clarify your understanding of the position in relation to incidents of that sort by putting to you the substance of one or two comments that you've made about it in the past. First of all, is it right that it was generally difficult to assess who was responsible for those killings?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: There were rumours to suggest that Serbs were the perpetrators as well as rumours to suggest the reverse?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both rumours were abounded, depending on who you were talking to, yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And is it right that you took the view some of these crimes might be related to ordinary criminal activity or mafia activity associated with Peje or Pec?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And also that you would always have in mind the fact that blood vengeance or blood feuds were a factor that often resulted in deaths in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is also correct, and I think it was a point one tried to impress upon people that this was a way of life, whether we liked it or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Those are my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Emmerson. In view of the fact that Mr. Guy-Smith has no questions, Mr. Harvey you'll now have an opportunity to cross-examine Mr. Crosland.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Crosland.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I represent Lahi Brahimaj, who is the gentleman sitting immediately behind me. Just a couple of questions essentially. I'd like to focus on your role in looking for information about General Staffs. Would it be fair to say that as the Defence Attache you had a very good knowledge of the operations of the General Staff of the Serb army, the Yugoslav Army?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect, sir, that's a very wide-ranging question. I was accredited, as you correctly indicated, to the Vojska Jugoslavije. Our business, whether formal or informal or social, was controlled by the foreign liaison service, a part of the General Staff. And as is usual in most countries, the Defence Attache element would be briefed by the General Staff, as appropriate to the situation which arose at the time. So, yes, I was in contact with the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And one of your functions was to obtain as much information as you could about the operations of the Serb security forces, both army and the various wings of the police on the ground in Kosovo, that's -- I think you've testified to already?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. By dint of, I was allowed access to these areas, and I thinkI have indicated in my previous statements that this I don't think is usual, possibly because we attempted to give a fair and broad picture of what was going on in Kosovo itself and possibly it was of use to the Vojska Jugoslavije General Staff in attempting to sort this problem out.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: In reporting, as you did, extensively to your own government on what you found on the ground and what you learned from your contacts with the Serbian forces, Yugoslav forces, you were also concerned, as you've told us, to get as much reliable information as you could about the other side in Kosovo; namely, the KLA?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir, in order to try and give a more balanced picture of this problem that initiated, as I said already, in 1996/1997, and then it came in -- began in earnest in 1998 and into 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: During the 1998 period with which we're concerned primarily here, that's March through to the end of September, you've told us you made numerous visits to Kosovo there almost once a week I think. And during that time, did you attempt to make contact with anything that could be called a General Staff on the side of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: We visited several KLA headquarters; and in these headquarters, I think Crni Lug, Malisevo, and obviously in the Dukadjin area, Glodjane, we met several people who were purported to be of General Staff rank. At that time information as to the exact nature of the background structure of the KLA was fairly vague.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: You've made a number of statements in this case. I'm not going to take you through them specifically, but would you accept this line from a statement that you gave in June of 2006: "The KLA was organised, but to call the body at the top a 'General Staff' might be misnaming it."

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: The phrase is correct; and as I've said in other statements, I'm always having had to carry out various operations against other counter-revolutionary forces. One is never very keen to give them more credit than they may or may not have and to try and work on facts rather than on fiction, but that is my own personal view, not a particularly a Ministry of Defence view. But one is trying to, as I said, keep things in perspective; and if the situation develops and you can see where the developments are going, then obviously one applies common sense and says, Okay, we now have - I think I called it - a fledgling organisation. But during 1998, it became a much more organised operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: You've indicated on many occasions that Kosovo was a very fluid situation throughout much of 1998. You would confirm that, I take it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: The KLA suffered a number of very substantial reversals, particularly through the period May to September of 1998. Would you agree with that as well?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we described yesterday in court, that is when the Serbs mounted I suppose one of their first major offensives, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And was it your view that the KLA was not tactically well-organised to resist the -- the might of those Serb offensives?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, sir, it was quite clear from the documents produced yesterday that the Serbs had the potential overwhelming forces to have mounted any operation they wished. I can't answer the question as to why they did not do that, but I think I would agree that the Serbs had the capability.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Would you also agree that the KLA only really started to regroup in a reasonably organised fashion - and I understand that's obviously a matter of definition - but in a reasonably organised fashion some time after the major offensive of September of 1998?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree with that and I think I've made that statement. It seemed that they had a resupply of both men and materiel, and we saw a growing -- confidence may be the wrong word, but certainly an ability to stand their ground, again, against far superior forces or potentially far superior forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Did you ever meet anybody who you were told was the Chief of the KLA General Staff during this period? Again, I'm dealing March through September.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I can recall, sir, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as specifically saying he was the Chief of the General Staff, no. I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Did you know the name of the KLA's Chief of General Staff at that time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether General Ceku, as he then was, I don't know. That was a name that was bandied about, but I don't think with any great credibility from my level, and I stress from my level.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I understand also that I'm taxing a very good memory; but over a long period of time, it may be difficult to remember who was in what position at what stage. I see you nodding?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: You said in one of your other statements: "Based on my dealings with the KLA and knowledge of many of their operations, I do not think that its General Staff had particularly effective control over the organisation." Does that summarize the view that you've really already just given us this morning, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I would agree with that statement, based on the sightings that we had of the KLA, which is perhaps difficult for the Court to understand. You are operating in a very demanding and quite dangerous situation in which, not unnaturally, when I was driving around in a red or maroon Defender with a big Union Jack all over it, it was fairly easy to recognise and, therefore, could quite easily lead a trail to a possible KLA headquarters which the Serbs could well have followed up. And, therefore, meetings were difficult to plan, and the KLA were naturally quite secretive and understandably so about their operations and the personnel who were controlling these operations. And so I go back to the point I made initially, that the organisation of battle of the KLA, from my point of view, was actually very quite difficult to come across. One came across various commanders, as I've indicated in my reports, who controlled areas. And I think at the time, if my memory is correct, they themselves indicated that they were not on their own, but there was not a great deal of coordinated control at that particular time. Now, I may be wrong in that assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: It would certainly be my submission that you're absolutely right in that assessment, but could I just take you one stage further. In another of your statements, you made this observation: "I am unaware of the existence of any KLA doctrine or the ability of the organisation to impose discipline, especially that related to criminal acts and their prevention; nor am I aware whether any KLA commanders ever ordered criminal attacks." Does that sound familiar, and is that something you stand by today, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I would stand by that particular statement. I think the military action and criminal activity were undoubtedly interwoven, as we all know, within the Albanian society. The control, as I've indicated, is probably very difficult to -- or certainly from my point of view, very difficult to ascertain.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: But, again, you also stand by the point that you are not aware whether any KLA commanders ever did order criminal attacks?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I can't specifically state that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Thank you. You also, I think, indicated that at an early stage, relatively speaking, you did visit a place called Jablanica. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reason I'm hesitating, sir, is because I think there are actually two Jablanicas, so I'm not certain which one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: You're quite right, there are.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Though there may well be more, but there are at least two, so which one are you indicating, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Well, I would be indicating the one which was on a main supply route for the KLA, coming from the Albanian border through on into Drenica. Does that ring a bell with you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it's the Jablanica up towards the area of Klina or not that far from Klina, then I do recall I think we visited it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Perhaps we better have the map in front of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Could we have P10, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Sorry. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And if you look towards the right-hand east side of the map, north-east quadrant, do you see Jablanica there? There's a large O.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do, sir, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: That's the one to which I'm referring. To your recollection, is that the one that you believe that you visited?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it is, sir, yeah. I may be mistaken, but I think, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And, please, tell me if this is something that is too far back for you to have any clear recollection of, but do you recall whether there was a KLA presence at the time that you visited that Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it's the area that we visited, there were a few KLA there, as I recall; but I, as I said - and forgive me - I may be mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Do you remember approximately when it was you made that visit, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think - and this is a guesstimate - sometime in March, April, May. I think it -- I think it came about from having visited people in the Drenica, Vocnjak, and then we moved down towards this one, I think, but I may be mistaken. I can't be more accurate than that, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: That's fair. Do you recall making this statement: "I do not remember whether I was ever told that there were detention camps in Glodjane or Jablanica"?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I recall making that statement, and I would stand by that particular statement, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: You recall that you don't recall is what it comes to?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed, Colonel Crosland. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, before Mr. Re re-examines, there is one answer that the witness gave on page 7, lines 11 and 12, which in my submission would benefit from clarification. In answering Mr. Harvey's question at lines 11 and 12, Colonel Crosland drew a distinction between the KLA as a fledgling organisation, a description he's used on a number of occasions, and the KLA as a much more organised operation, and indicated that it was during 1998 that it changed from one to the other. And I wonder if it might be of assistance to the Trial Chamber to have Colonel Crosland say when it was during 1998 that that transition was effected in his view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if it is possible to give a point in time. Mr. Crosland.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think I made a statement, and I think the time I said that I perceived a more organised element was probably in the earlier autumn, September/October time. I think that -- I think that ties-in with my previous statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that's also you have no reason at this moment to deviate in any way from the previous statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I don't. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Re, I do understand that there is need to re-examine the witness. You have an opportunity to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Good morning again, Colonel Crosland. I have several things I wish to ask you about, following your cross-examination by Mr. Emmerson yesterday. The first thing, if you could perhaps turn to a document which is labelled, which is behind tab 14 there, which is actually Exhibit D70. You were asked some questions about this particular document yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's a VJ document, and it can be publicly displayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I indicate for Mr. Re's assistance and for the assistance of Your Honours and the witness, we've now got the official translation available, and I think it's been uploaded into the system and will be substituted for the draft translation that exists. I was going to deal with that at housekeeping at the end; but if Mr. Re is going to cross-examine -- I'm sorry, re-examine in relation to that document, it may be of assistance to everybody to have the final translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'd be very grateful. Is there a hard copy which I could use?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: We have several hard copies available.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Perhaps I can hand three for the Chamber, two for the registry, one for the witness, and one for Mr. Re. There will not at the moment be copies for the translators, but I'm -- it may be that Madam Registrar has already made the substitution so that the correct translation will appear on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Colonel, have you --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've got the document, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- the new or the final translation.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I want to take you to paragraph 1, which is on the first page, and where it says: "Task: In coordinated action with neighbouring forces of the Republic of Serbia MUP break up Siptar/Albanian/DTG/sabotage and terrorist groups/and secure supply routes for the VJ units." This is a document, an order, issued on the 16th May 1998 by Colonel Dragan Zivanovic, Chief of Staff of the 125th Motorised Brigade. The question is: What is the significance of this particular task, that is, to secure supply routes for VJ units in terms of the operations you observed and the conflicts you observed between the KLA and the Serbian forces in that period?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, as I've indicated, sir, that there are very view routes, Tarmac routes, through the area of Kosovo; and in particular in the western area of the province, the major route north to south was from Pec through Decani, Djakovica, and down to Prizren. And I presume from -- I presume from this tasking here that this is the secure -- or the task here is to secure this particular supply route as the main supply route to western Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was the significance of that for the VJ in terms of the conflict that was then occurring?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, as I've indicated to the Court, the border area with Albania was more or less like a sieve, in that men and supplies were coming through from Albania as and when they could get them through; and, therefore, this road back from the border about -- on approximately 20 to 25 kilometres from the border, I have called before the red line, along which the Serb security forces attempted to provide a secondary blocking position before the KLA could distribute the supplies onward towards the Drenica and other areas of operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: At 4638 of the transcript yesterday and around that -- around then, Mr. Emmerson asked you about operations that the VJ and the MUP were conducting against the KLA operatives, and he suggested that you would not need to have paramilitary anti-terrorist police on the ground, or at least snipers being able to take shots at KLA operatives. And you answered: "With respect, sir, that is one way of" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think it would be much more helpful if Mr. Re were to take us to the actual question and answer, because the way that that is put, in line 18, is that I suggested that you would not need to have paramilitary anti-terrorist police on the ground, or at least snipers. Now, I'm not quite sure even what the grammar of that sentence means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there's any objection against the way in which previous testimony is reflected, the party putting the question to the witness is invited to quote literally. If you have the lines, Mr. Re, I have the text in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I simply put the not before -- I'll rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The question you were asked was: "You would need, would you not, either to have paramilitary anti-terrorist police operating on the ground, or at the very least snipers to take shots at the KLA operatives?" And you answered: "With respect, sir, that's one way of doing it. There are many ways of doing an encircling document." What are the other ways, based upon your experience in conflicts and counter-insurgency, of doing an encirclement?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: So, again, it's a very wide question. The tactics involved in dealing with counter-insurgency go from the very simple to the extremely complex, based on intelligence and/or the chance meeting with counter-insurgency forces. I think the point I was trying to make to Mr. Emmerson is that snipers are useful if you have the opportunity target. If you do not encircle an area which you are attempting to assault or maybe just to go and visit and find intelligence, then if people are frightened, and many people were frightened in Kosovo, they would then run away, whether they were actively involved with the KLA or not. So I don't know whether I've helped the answer or complicated it, to be honest.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your answer went on that there was what you would call the heavy -- "the very heavy option of using ordinary troops or perhaps a more precise operation of encircling with the use of aircraft and helicopters, rather than what I would call a direct assault, which was more likely the norm of the Serbian forces." What I'd like you to do is expand a little on that where you said: "Which was more likely the norm of the Serbian forces." What do you mean by the "norm of the Serbian forces" in terms of what you observed and experienced in your visits to Kosovo and the intelligence information you received about what the Serbian forces were doing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before Mr. Crosland answers this question, I'd like to be perfectly clear about what was "more likely the norm," because the answer was "the very heavy option of using ordinary troops or perhaps a more precise option of encircling with the use of aircraft and helicopters, rather than what I would call a direct assault, which was more likely the norm of the Serbian forces." Now, was the direct assault more likely the norm of the Serbian forces or was it the very heavy option using ordinary troops or perhaps a more precise operation of encircling with the use of aircraft and helicopters, was that more likely the norm of Serbian forces? I'd like to know exactly what you meant before you further explain what exactly you meant by "the norm of the Serbian forces."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I think from my reports and from the orders we have seen from the Vojska Jugoslavije, there were very heavy and direct forces used to mount most of these operations, which also encompassed special forces from both the VJ and from the MUP and the RDB. The Serbs had very few helicopters, and I recall only seeing one during my time in Kosovo. So that particular type of operation was not available to them. They, therefore, resorted to what I would call a very heavy-handed operation, which normally involved artillery or indirect mortar fire as a prelude to any assault which had the effect of chasing out the civilian population in most cases without any casualties, although this was difficult to ascertain. But from the displaced personnel that we talked to, most villagers seemed to get away before the assault proper went into the objective area. And so I think I would say that the majority of the assaults were heavy and direct, using the variety of forces that I have indicated, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And how did you assess the overall effectiveness of those tactics used by the Serb forces against the KLA?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I think I've said on many occasions, the wanton destruction by Serb security forces throughout the province of Kosovo can only have driven the civilian population against their activities, whether they were either for the KLA or not. But if your house is burned down, your petrol station ravaged, your crops burned, your livestock shot, I don't think it endears you to the people doing these actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If you can turn to --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Unless Your Honours have anything more on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I have a long question which is already for a long time on my mind, as a matter of fact, and I tried to find a proper definition. You, as many others, are using the word or the expression "artillery." Now, many people in the past have been able to tell me that certain weaponry was artillery, but where exactly artillery stops and becomes something else. So a clear definition until now, I don't recall that I ever received that. But I'll try again since you're using the expression "artillery," Mr. Crosland. Could you help me out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will try, Your Honour. I'm not an artillery man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the beginning of the answer of almost everyone. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And you raise an interesting question because the Serbian word differentiates itself between various calibres, but I will not go into that detail because I think it will ... Artillery, in my experience and knowledge, is designed to be fired from a calibre of approximately 100-millimetre upwards to 155-millimetre, where in the case of 155-millimetre projectile, which has got a huge range, can produce a hole in the ground about 5 metres by 5 metres. So you have got a considerable -- it's a 90-pound shell, I think, and it will do considerable damage to, obviously, human beings and property. The smaller calibres from 105 upwards are obviously producing, still damaging effects, particularly if fired directly at housing or at human beings, obviously. But artillery is used usually in three- or six-gun groups so that you have what we call a battery or a half-battery ability to fire, and it's an area weapon. It is precise, but it also has a spread of range, which means if you aimed it at a village, you would hit several houses within that village itself, and that may be spread over a hundred metres or more. It depends on the equipment, how well the equipment is maintained and where the equipment is firing from, if it is in a proper location, dug-in, and the guns are what we call well surveyed in. So they are stable; and when they are fired, they don't move around too much. The movement of these guns will, obviously, give you a further spread of shot into the target area. Above 155-millimetre, as far as I'm aware, there may be one or two other calibres; but in this particular confrontation, we then went to rocket-propelled artillery, which is 122-millimetre, a smaller calibre, but with a longer range, but also with the same degree of spread at the objective end. I hope that helps, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So I do understand that artillery is characterised more or less by calibre, use of the weaponry, effect. I'm just summarizing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's what we call indirect fire, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's controlled by people forward. It can be used in a direct role. If you can see the target, you can then fire directly at it. But it's what we call line of sight. So if there is a hill in the way, you have to elevate the barrel to allow you to fire over the hill. And we have mortars that are then smaller calibre than that to be able to fire over a hill or whatever happens to be in the way of the line of sight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So it's a combination of calibre, use, effect, and, of course, distance related to calibre, which finally qualifies the use of certain weaponry as artillery?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Colonel Crosland, can you please turn to tab 24 in the documents, which is D77, which is a report under the hand of Colonel Vladimir Lazarevic, dated the 15th of July, 1998, from the Pristina forward command post to various subordinate units. At page 4645, yesterday, Mr. Emmerson briefly took you to this particular document and referred you to paragraph 7 on the first page, which just says: "From today on for the next seven days, the KLA is planning to attack the VJ in the Radonjic Lake sector as the VJ's deployment there is preventing them from achieving their aims." My question is simply that from reading that document, are you able to say what the Lake Radonjic or Radonjic Lake sector is? I'm just asking you from reading that document, not referring to anything else.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: So from what I understand, the inference is that Lake Radonjic, as was shown yesterday, was a major Serb deployment area. And this, obviously, influenced the ability of the KLA to move through this area as a supply route to further operational areas to the east in the Drenica and beyond. So I could understand the KLA wanting to stir-up problems in the area, to try and break the attention of the Serbian security forces whilst they carried out their own operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What I'm asking you is just to confine and concentrate on the words "Lake Radonjic" or "Radonjic Lake sector." From that document are you able to say, just looking at the document, what the Lake Radonjic sector actually is, just from looking at the document, nothing else?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I understand your question credibility, sir, it was a Serbian VJ deployment area. I'm sorry. I don't quite follow you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: From reading the document, can you say what the sector is? Does the document indicate anywhere what the sector actually is and what it's referring to and what area it covers?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apart from Lake Radonjic, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: At page 4671, yesterday, Mr. Emmerson asked you about attacks by the Serbian forces on Irzniq and the question was: "But it was your understanding that they would periodically launch and overrun Rznic over that summer period. Is that right?" And you answered: "That's correct, yes." I am after a clarification by what you understood "periodically" to mean.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, sir, we're talking about Prilep and Irzniq. Rznic seems to have crept in somewhere and I don't quite understand, whether that's a misquote on my part --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It's be may helpful for the witness to know it's another pronunciation. Rznic and Irzniq are the same place.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. As I said yesterday on many times, sir, when the KLA attacked the main supply route, from Pec through Decani down to Djakovica past Prilep and Irzniq, then there would be retaliatory attacks by the Serb security forces on either an opportunity basis or, as we heard yesterday, in May on a major basis where several axes were in the orders or the written orders, were indicating that units would clear these axes. Now, whether they cleared them or not is open for discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When you were asked yesterday about your understanding that they would periodically launch and overrun Rznic or Irzniq, what I'm trying to get at is what did you understand by "periodically" when you answered "that's correct."

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think exactly what I've just said is that the MUP had a check-point on the main road that was hit many times and several people were killed there, and they would retaliate into the surrounding area, which, you know, I would totally understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And from when you say "overrun," are you saying there's a difference between taking territory and controlling it and overrunning territory?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, very much, sir. I think I hopefully made -- tried to make clear to the Court that the situation was very fluid throughout this period and ground was -- villages may be attacked, areas of tactical importance may be taken for a short time, and then not held. And , therefore, the situation ebbed and flowed rather like the tide coming in on the beach.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are you able to say with any precision how many times the Serbian forces overran Irzniq in that period?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say with any consistency, I mean apart from the fact that in the end both villages were extremely badly damaged, as I've indicated in my reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are you able to give an approximation, one, two, 10, 20, five, or whatever?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not entirely, sir, because, you know, I physically could not be there throughout the entire period. We saw the damage accumulating throughout 1998 and into 1999, and that was the effect of several assaults that took place. But to try and put a number on it, I'm afraid I cannot, a specific number, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do Your Honours have any questions about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yesterday Mr. Emmerson asked you about the -- what you observed at the lake when you went there in September -- on the 8th of September, 1998. And at page 4681, he reminded you of your essential position that you told the Serb authorities that they needed a -- to provide to the international community evidence of a "clean-gloves" forensic investigation. My follow-up for clarification on that is: Were you aware or what was your understanding of the forensic equipment and facilities available to the Serbs in that area at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I have no idea what capability they had. I just asked them that in order to provide prima facie evidence as to who had done this particular act, it would neither help nor hinder their particular cause. But their ability came I presume under the MUP, to whom I was not accredited and, therefore, had no precise knowledge of.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You were also shown two documents, two VJ documents yesterday, at tabs 28 and 29. The first one is dated the 7th of August, 1998, and the second one is dated the 10th of August, 1998, and they relate to actions by the Serbian forces against the KLA. If you could turn to tab 29, which is D81 -- 82, I believe, and if you can turn to the first paragraph, it's an order of Lieutenant-General Pavkovic of the 10th of August, 1998, and where it says -- I'll just read the top and the bottom: "I have decided, with MUP and VJ forces, smash the DTS/sabotage-terrorist forces/stronghold and establish control over the general Crnobreg village," et cetera. Then down lines: "With the following aim, by attack and active operations against the flank and the rear, with diversionary operations and support from the VJ BG, smash and pull back the DTS from the Djakovica-Decane-Pec road, then destroy the enemy in the general Crnobreg village-Rznic village-Glodjane village-Babaloc village-Prilep area; and after that, capture this area and prevent further operations by the DTS." What I want to ask you about that is what sort of movement in military terms is that describing? What sort of operation is it describing?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said yesterday, it seems to be what we would call a commander's intent and a prelude to an operation order of a very heavy capability, and I think we then had other details which outlined the battle groups or combat groups that were to take part in this operation. And it appears clear from what General Pavkovic is stating here that he was determined to smash and push back the KLA from various areas, which is, I'm afraid, I suppose, standard military practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, at page 4657, suggested to you that that was an operation of encirclement, referring to one which you had described earlier. Now, before you answer the question, I want you to have a look at the map of the area - you're looking at D32 - and the areas described in this particular exhibit. And I want you to describe the sort of operation, in terms of a push or an encirclement, the military terminology you would use to describe the actual movement, planned movement of troops?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Again, if Mr. Re is going to quote the transcript, he should quote the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: He should quote the witness's answer. The question was: "This was a question of encirclement, isn't it, of the kind you were describing earlier on." And the answer is: "That appears to be the case, yes, sir, yeah."

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I don't think there's any dispute about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I did not find where Mr. Re was not properly reflecting the testimony, but this is now on the record so, therefore, everyone agrees what the question was and what the answer was yesterday. The question today put to you by Mr. Re needs to be answered as well. Could you give an answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will try, Your Honour, yes. I'm a bit puzzled but now I am unclear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the question is not clear enough, we'll invite Mr. Re to make it more clear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had hoped that the answer I gave yesterday -- the commander's aims, as stated here, are, in my opinion, fairly clear. Now, there is a difference between the commander's intent, as the general commanding his troops, and as to what actually happens on the ground, which is quite natural. So the commander's intent is to carry out a major operation in this area to try and smash, in his words, the KLA influence within the area. Now, that, quite clearly, did not happen on the ground because, as I've attempted to inform the Court, the Serb security forces, for whatever reason, did not manage to hold or wish to hold ground that -- and there is certainly ground there which does dominate the area. But by purely sitting in an area without actively patrolling and controlling the area by vehicle check-points, by observation points that are looking and providing information, you don't control the ground. And the KLA were very active and good at bypassing Vojska Jugoslavije and MUP positions and using the ground and their local knowledge. So a very major operation was planned and presumably -- and did take place. The cause and effect of that operation was probably not worth the huge amount of effort that was put into it, for the reasons I have just outlined to you, sir. Does that help? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I was involuntarily shaking my head. What I'm actually getting at is when Mr. Emmerson said: "That is an operation of encirclement, isn't it" and you said: "That appears to be the case, yes." My recollection yesterday - and I will be corrected if I am wrong - is that Mr. Emmerson showed you the order; but before answering it, you didn't look at the map. So what I want you to do is look at the map and familiarise yourself with those villages and axes described. And in light of looking at the map, inform the Court whether it is, in fact, an encirclement as your answer yesterday was: "That appears to be the case."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: If I may say so, in order to answer that question, the witness needs to look at the tasks for units and to mark on the map the axes for each unit, so Gllogjan to Shaptej for the first one, Gramocelj to Babaloc to Rastavica for the second, Gramocelj to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least that's what you suggest Mr. Re would invite the witness to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Those are the tasks that would determine the answers to whether this comes out as an encirclement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether that should be done by marking on the map or looking at the map is another matter. But, Mr. Re, if you would follow that suggestion, the Chamber would certainly not oppose, and it might -- since it's a long list read by Mr. Emmerson yesterday, today read by you again, it might assist but I leave it up to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Of course, it would assist. It might have assisted yesterday if we had done it that way, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Today we always know better what we should have done yesterday. That's general experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Colonel, can you, first, familiarise yourself with those particular areas on the map, and then I'll get you to draw some lines on the computer. It will be D32 and it will be only the computer screen in front of you. It's probably better to familiarise yourself first on the hard copy.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then perhaps Madam Usher could assist the witness with the pen to mark. We are on D32. Mr. Re, I take it that you have chosen the size you would exactly need. Because you know once marking has started, zooming in and out becomes impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. I think all of these locations are marked on P10, which is a much clearer and smaller-scale map; and it may be for Mr. Re's purposes, it would be easier to follow it by simply loading P10 which covers, I think, all of the locations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time, P10, if nothing else, then D31 -- D32, but without the red markings on it and on a different scale. But zooming in and out might do as well, so I leave it up to you, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: D10 is probably better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D10, then we get D10 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It is, in fact, P10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, it is D10. Yes, I apologise. It takes a while to get the map uploaded.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, would you please carefully check whether everything you would like the witness to mark is on the screen at this moment or whether we need to zoom in and zoom out. It might be that it should be zoomed out a little bit or am I wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Everything is on the screen. Is it, Mr. Re?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Everything is on the screen. Okay. So that should be fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you see the Crnobreg village-Rznic village-Glodjane village-Gramocelj village-Prilep village sector?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt again. But if Mr. Re is asking about the encirclement question, he has to ask what instructions were issued to the forces, not which axes they were trying to break. And the instructions issued to the forces are under 2.1 to 2.5. And if each of those axes is marked on the map, we will then see what the manoeuvre was that was being ordered; whereas, if he asks the witness to mark a series of axes from paragraph 1, he's asking the witness to mark the targets, not the manoeuvres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, perhaps we could ask the witness whether he would agree that he has looked at the document before, whether he would agree that the tasks are set out, and that's of course what is suggested by the title in 2.1, in 2, and that the targets are found in 1.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may be able to help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Plainly the general who -- or his Chief of Staff who's written this particular paper would layout for the general rough axes as in, I have decided, paragraph. Specific tasks would then be allocated to various units. Whether you want -- whether you would like the specific tasks looked at or the axes that the general has asked to be cleared, I think probably in the end become one and the same thing,.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that should do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Otherwise, we're not doing what the general tells, and that usually means you're not getting very far up the promotion ladder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, what you say is what we find specified under 2 covers what we find in 1.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly, sir. The first paragraph, I believe, lays out the general direction that the general wants cleared. You then go down to the units, which are the tasks referred to under paragraph 2, that give each unit its specific objective tasks. It becomes slightly further complex, as I'm afraid only us in the military can do, is that if those objectives fall very quickly, then a unit will exploit further if the commander thinks the situation gives him that opportunity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Wouldn't it - and I'm suggesting this now to both parties - if we would ask Mr. Crosland by marking the map to illustrate what tasks were given under paragraph 2; and then once he's done this, to look at paragraph 1 and see whether there's anything left in paragraph 1 which would further illustrate what the order actually covers here. Would that be a good suggestion?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I would endorse that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And then one can see each manoeuvre as it builds up on the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I see that Mr. Re is nodding "yes" as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, Mr. Crosland, you are now invited on the basis of the specifications in 2, the tasks for the unit, to illustrate, I take it mainly by drawing the axis, on the map; and then once we've done that, to look at 1, whether this gives an incomplete picture or whether it gives a fair impression of what the order is about. Madam Usher could perhaps assist the witness when he uses the magic pen. Yes. You know that once you start writing on the screen it marks. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not known for my drawing capabilities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, there is a possibility to correct if you think you did anything wrong. So please proceed, and perhaps explain what you're marking, starting with I take it 2.1 then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. 2.1 is the battle group 52, with various forces, as outlined, starting from trig point 509, which I'm having difficulty in finding. But from 509, they go down to Glodjane. So they will presumably have started --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: 509 is just above Shaptej, if that helps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, there are two Shaptejs, Mr. Harvey, as you're aware of. Could you please look at just to the map. Yes, that's Shaptej. Just above what you marked is 509.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, right sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You see that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I wonder if we might ask the witness to mark these axes as Your Honour indicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: In other words, to mark the line between the two points rather than so to simply, so to speak, underlining the two spots and that way we will see the picture building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you could follow that suggestion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will try, sir. This appears to have started from Saptej and going north towards Glodjane. Paragraph 2.2, sir, comes from Gramocelj to Babaloc and the Rastavica axis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you could mark that axis on the map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we have Babaloc, Gramocelj, and I'm now looking for the third one, Rastavica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would look a bit north-west --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, I see it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- I think that -- and if you could mark the axis, so that's the line connecting these three locations. Now, we move to the 2.3 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- which is subdivided.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- which is again from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Although 2.3.1 is followed not by 2.3.2, so it's just 2.3, I take it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, from Gramocelj to Glodjane.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please mark that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So we have Gramocelj down here through Dubrava, this village here, and to Glodjane, which are already marked, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you could try to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So I presume it is this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then take it up to Glodjane.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And then towards ... 2.4 is appearing to be coming along the -- if I remember rightly, there was some woods over on the west side of the road in Drenovacke, up here, and then it comes down along here through Prilep and on into Rznic; and then further down, towards Glodjane. 2.5 is from Crnobreg village up in the north, as indicated. The task is to secure their left flank from Beleg, and that appears to be as far as they go. I would have thought, sir, Your Honours, that that indicates an encompassing assault in that you have troops coming from the south, from Dubrava, towards Glodjane. You have a further axis from Drenovac through Prilep, Rznic, back south to Glodjane, with flanking projection. Now, that's what the orders say. Whether that happened, of course, is another matter, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I wonder, in the light of that answer, whether Mr. Re would put this question again whether this is properly described as an encirclement.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I mean, there is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson. Mr. Emmerson. Mr. Re is re-examining the witness. There's no need to act as -- I don't know as a matter of fact how they call that in English, but in the French they say it's the "souffleur," as on the bottom of the stage if someone loses his text.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It's a prompt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think Mr. Re heard your question. We were not yet there where the witness, as we was invited to do, as to see whether what he marked on the map gives a fair picture of what we find under 1 or whether anything has to be added, and then we'll first leave it to Mr. Re to put his question.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. Please proceed, Mr. Re, I would like to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Colonel Crosland, you've now marked on the map this axis described or the battle -- or the plans described in that particular order. Based on your experience, what sort of manoeuvre or operation is this in military terms?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a manoeuvre operation. It's not a -- it's not a complete encirclement. Because if you look on the map the KLA, certainly if I was the KLA, I would not have stayed in Glodjane. I would have gone east. Therefore, you can say it is not a complete encircle operation. I think we have to understand -- if I may suggest to the Court, one has to understand that if you are facing the type of odds that the KLA were facing in May of this year in this particular operation, then you would be very foolish to stand and fight against very superior opposition that is currently deployed on the map. Therefore, time is on the side of the terrorist. He withdraws probably to the east. I can't answer that question because, A, I was not there; and any gentleman who probably can answer it is Mr. Haradinaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Colonel, I just wish to clarify something before I finish with this exhibit. You've drawn a line, a red line, from Drenovac, from west to east, and then going down the road south, and then across the top of Prilep towards Rznic with an arrow; and then another arrow comes down from Rznic to Glodjane and that's going south, and other arrows are coming up from Dubrava-Saptej area. I'm trying to work out -- by that, are you meaning Serb forces were to come from Drenovac, down the road, across to Prilep, up to Rznic, and then go down to Glodjane, or are you describing something else?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are the tasks that have been laid out in paragraph 2. I've drawn them on the map. As I indicated to the Court, what actually happened on the ground depends on the situation and how much resistance was given or acted against the Serb security forces on their approach would depend on how far they came down. And, obviously, they don't want to start firing at one another when they meet, if they met, in Glodjane itself. So what is drawn, I come back to the point I'm making, you can have the best plan and the most detailed tasks in the world; but on contact, a plan generally goes out the window because there is an enemy who doesn't particularly want to get killed on the other side or involved. And in this case, they may have decided not to oppose the Serb forces, as I've indicated, who are far superior and to stay and fight another day.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Those are my questions on this exhibit. Just in terms of time, there's just one other area I wish to ask the Colonel about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but we'd rather do that after the break. I take it that it will take you some time; and for the interpreters and for the transcribers, it's time to have some rest. We will have a break, Mr. Crosland, and we'll most likely not continue long after the break, but we'll resume at five minutes past is 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, should that be saved and given an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it should be saved. We can do it now or after the break. Let's do it now, unless there's no further marking needed. Madam Registrar, the marked map, P10, would now have number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit Number P323, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Can we get this already admitted into evidence. Maps usually take a short-cut. Yes, admitted into evidence. We have a break until five minutes past 11.00

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Colonel Crosland, yesterday, Mr. Emmerson took you to tab 28, which is Exhibit D80 or 81. I've just lost my index.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 28 is 81, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's D81 which is a report of the Pristina Corps command, dated the 7th of August, 1998. If you could just turn to that, please. Yesterday, Mr. Emmerson asked you about the document; and at page 4654 to 4655 of the transcript, he read to you paragraph 1 of the report, which is under the hand of Colonel Mladen Cirkovic describing: "Between 25th of July and 6th August, 1998, MUP units were engaged by decision of the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija along the following axes," and then describes some axes. What I want you to do is to look at the axes which are described.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If a fresh Exhibit of P10 could be placed on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'll take you to that in a moment. Now, if you look at the axes, this Komorane village-Lapusnik village-Kijevo village, those are not in the Dukagjin area. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And is it -- is it the case that the only ones from those axes described in that paragraph which are actually in the Dukadjin area are Gradjanica, Bandera, trig point 490, and Glodjane village?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And we noted earlier that there is another Jablanica, which is in the Peje area -- I'm sorry. I suppose you described it as the Klina area between Klina and Peje, and that's not the one we're referring to here. What I want you to do is look at this report - and this is a report of military actions - and I want you to look at the map. And, firstly, you're aware, aren't you, that there are two Glodjanes. There is one referred to as the Catholic Glodjane?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And there's the Glodjane which is from where Mr. Haradinaj originates?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand that, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Now, yesterday, it was described to you that the axis described there was one going to the non-Catholic Glodjane, that is, Mr. Haradinaj's Glodjane, and I don't think you were given an opportunity to look at the map when Mr. Emmerson, who will of course correct me if I am wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It isn't that. It's just in order to find these positions that Mr. Re is asking about, he'll need D32 and not P10. They don't appear on P10, all of them, but they do appear on D32.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's why the reason I've got D32 in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: As far as I can see, they're all on P10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The other Glodjanes are but, of course, you also refer to Klina, and that's, of course, only on D32. But the other Glodjane are on this map, on D -- on P10, Mr. Emmerson. So if we limit it to that and not to the Klina, as you said before, then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm only interested in the ones that are relevant to the Dukagjin area and the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you see the two Glodjanes, the Catholic Glodjane which is on the road from Peje to I think Nepolje?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've got that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Now, what I would like you to do is read the report which you have in your hand there and to look at the map, the axis: Gradjanica-Bandera (trig point 490)-Glodjane-Jablanica village, and from your understanding, your military understanding, to draw on the map the axis which is described there.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understand it correct, sir -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps, Mr. Re, if you would specifically point at the axis you want him to mark so he knows exactly, because it's a long list under number 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Only relating to those at the end of the paragraph it says: "Gradjanica village-Bandera (trig point 490)-Gllogjan village-Jablanica." In military terms, those axes described, can you please mark, from your understanding, of what they are on this map -- on the plan?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gradjanica at the top here, down towards Bandera, point 490, which I'm now underlining. I beg your pardon. Down to Glodjane and then on down to Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And to make it clear, on the map you have marked the Catholic Glodjane, not Mr. Haradinaj's Glodjane?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, as I understand it, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the marking is done, then a number should be assigned to it. Madam Registrar, that would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit Number P324, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I just want to clarify: When you were asked yesterday, at page 4655, Mr. Emmerson asked you about the second axis.
