Your answer: "That's possible, yes." It goes down and you say: "The second one," as you stated, "between Glodjane and Jablanica which is a lot vaguer because the two are in cross-country area?" "Q. Yes." "A. Which could have gone cross the canal area? "Q. Yes. "A. It may not have done. I don't know. Now, having drawn that on the map, does that clarify in your own in mind whether the axis which Mr. Emmerson was describing to you went from Gradjanica to Catholic Glodjane to Jablanica or, in fact, from Jablanica right across to Mr. Haradinaj's Glodjane?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: So, I understood we were talking about, if I may refer to it, Mr. Haradinaj's home in Glodjane across to Jablanica and not what I would call the northern Glodjane. So that is the axis that I understood that Mr. Emmerson was talking about; but if I've got it wrong, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just seek to see whether there's really disagreement about this among the parties. Mr. Emmerson, usually, the axis are described with rather great precision. That means points of reference not too far from each other --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- to leave matters clear as where the axis are.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, Glodjane-Jablanica here would be a huge distance without clear reference. Therefore, if we are talking about Gradjanica-Bandera-Glodjane-Jablanica, in the system of describing axis, that at first makes more sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I agree, the order makes more sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Obviously, none of us is in a position to know for certain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But the order in which the villages appear would make more sense if the axis is as drawn by Colonel Crosland --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- than if it was a reference to Glodjane on the western side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And understood that way, the axis between Glodjane and Jablanica would, although cross water, not the canal --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- because it seems that it is the [indiscernible] which is crossed but not understood that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, first of all, may I say yes. There were two separate lines of questioning to Colonel Crosland in that regard. One in general terms - and I haven't got the transcript reference - was that for the KLA to retreat eastwards from Glodjane to Jablanica, that would involve them crossing the canal by and large. And, therefore, if you wish to cut-off their retreat, you would be militarily wise to ensure that they could not do that. And in that regard --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's a different --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- a somewhat -- sorry. Whilst I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What I'd like not to do now is start commenting and interpreting the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The point yesterday whether there was any disagreement about that between the parties because then we might have to explore that it in further detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: May I indicate that there is one further matter at some point I would like to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We first give an opportunity to Mr. Re to finish his re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The next question Mr. Emmerson asked was after Mr. Crosland said, "It may have not done it. I don't know." Mr. Emmerson said, "But the canal area does, does it not, flow right through the most direct route from Glodjane to Jablanica?" "A. It does. "Q. That very axis? "A. Yes." Which in that context could only be referring to that long axis in that order, because he was asking about that order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that is now in dispute and that's clarified, and what it takes to go from one place to another, apart from what Mr. Crosland tells us about it, can be verified on maps as well, and the Chamber will certainly do so. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nothing further. Then any need for --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Before Your Honours ask any further questions, may I just raise one matter. In answer to Mr. Re and commenting on the markings that the witness put on P10, which became P -- sorry, which became P323, Colonel Crosland said at page 36, line 5 of the transcript that the formation he had marked as a planned operation for the 10th of August was not -- I'll just read the passage: "It's not a complete encirclement. Because if you look on the map, the KLA, certainly if I was the KLA, I would not have stayed in Glodjane. I would have gone east. Therefore, you can say that it is not a complete encircle operation." And a few lines further down, on line 13, the answer continued: "Therefore, time is on the side of the terrorists. He withdraws probably to the east." Now, if one looks at the chronology, the axis that the witness has now marked is derived from tab 28, which is, for the record --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 7th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. D28, which is dated the 7th of August and describing activity which had taken place by the 6th of August; in other words, that Serbian deployment coming in a southerly direction towards Jablanica. I wanted to ask the witness whether, in light of the fact that there was a plainly Serbian advance just three days before the 10th of August, which was coming down towards Grabanica down towards Jablanica, and therefore effectively putting Serbian troops on that eastern flank, whether that is, in fact, would have closed the circle by preventing an escape in an easterly direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Crosland, I take it you've understood the question. If you'd like to have a closer look at your markings at the previous one, you can ask Madam Registrar to show you, because I take it you've now got the axis Grabanica-Bandera-Glodjane-Jablanica well in your memory. If you would like to look at the other one, please ask.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, I'm happy with the question as I understand it. As I said to the Court earlier on, I still don't -- I accept what Mr. Emmerson says, saying forces are moving down towards Jablanica and, therefore, providing in military terms a stop to the KLA moving east, but there is still a considerable distance some -- I believe these squares a kilometre squares. So approximately from Glodjane, Mr. Haradinaj's home, to Jablanica is about ten, 12 kilometres. That is a considerable area for forces to disappear into, and the area is, as indicated on the map, quite wooded and hilly. And, therefore, I would suggest that the encirclement is not complete if the forces stopped at Jablanica, as indicated by this order. So there is plenty of space for the KLA to disappear in the middle of the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the only way I can think of helping this particular question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, of course, it's good to -- that our attention is drawn to the military plans put on paper. Of course, you also have to pay attention to what actually happened on the ground, as you have drawn our attention to a number of times. And, finally, whether it qualifies as a full encirclement, yes or no, might not be the full and decisive factor for the whole of this case. Any further questions triggered by the questions Mr. Re? I see no request for further questions. Judge Hoepfel has a question for you

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes. Sir, may I get back to your answer you gave in connection with your visit at the canal area in September 1998. You testified in response to the question of Mr. Re, who had asked about -- just a moment. Page 24, line 24 -- who had asked: "What, in your understanding, was the forensic equipment and facilities availability to the Serbs in that area at that time?" Do you remember that was the question? And your answer had been: "Sir, I have no idea what capability they had. I just asked them that in order to provide prima facie evidence as to who had done this particular act," and so on. My question would be: When you asked them that, when you gave them this advice to provide prima facie evidence, was that before or on that day of your visit?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it was at the end of the -- of that particular visit. My remark was made to one of the MUP officers, one of the senior MUP officers. The suggestion was that that was the route that they should follow in order to properly identify who had committed this particular crime. Because as you are well aware, sir, there were unfortunately crimes being committed all over Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. I appreciate that. This answers my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Crosland, since I've got no further questions for you, and since you've answered all the questions put to you by the parties and the Bench, I'd like to thank you for not only for coming, for even coming twice. Usually, we excuse the witness already when we are dealing with exhibits; but perhaps since quite a number and if you would be willing to just stay and watch and assist us if there would be any need to do so in the administration of exhibits, then that would be highly appreciate. So I asked Madam Registrar to make a list, and she's printing it out now, with all the exhibits which were introduced during the testimony of Mr. Crosland.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think Your Honour should have the index now with -- as of first thing this morning, with all of the exhibit numbers that were ascribed during the day yesterday inserted, so that those which have not yet had identification numbers ascribed to them can be dealt with now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps we -- I don't know whether they were all used, that's of course the first thing that would have to be verified because the mere fact that they appear on your list, Mr. Emmerson, is not good enough to assign a number. But it might especially be earlier that ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll do it in the following way, Mr. Emmerson. There are a few documents on your index which have not been assigned MFI numbers yet. We'll leave them for the moment because there are two possibilities: Either they were not assigned them at the time or they were not used. We'll ask you and your team together with Madam Registrar to identify, not at this very moment, but out of court, to see whether there are any documents used but not yet assigned numbers. Madam Registrar then will prepare an additional list. And as far as we are concerned at this very moment, we'll just focus only on documents that have already been assigned a number. So we leave it open whether later today or tomorrow we'll have a short additional list of those documents not yet assigned numbers, but nevertheless used.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But we'll have to verify that first.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The fact is that the vast majority of those that were not ascribed numbers were, in fact, used, but there are a handful; that is, three or four or five that were not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have to verify that precisely and then make an additional list and at this moment focus only on those documents that have been assigned numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then Madam Registrar is about to print the list for me. Mr. Crosland, these are administrative matters that are really important but this sometimes takes some time. Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In relation to the Prosecution's exhibits with Mr. Crosland, we notified the Chamber in advance of -- there were two sets. There was the Limaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I'll take care of that. That's P92.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the full set of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's try to see whether we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we sorted out now everything. I start, not as usual, with D exhibits. D exhibits assigned numbers start with D36.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to rise to my feet. Is Your Honour starting from the lowest to the highest?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think D34 should be on the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but, of course, we have admitted already some. But Madam Registrar will immediately, D34, check that and I'll also check that on my computer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps you'll check, Mr. Emmerson, but it's related to another witness according to Madam Registrar. I asked her to give me --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well. That may well be right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So then I have D36 which is a map marked by Mr. Crosland, taken from D32. Then we jump to -- but I've some -- I still have to see whether that's correct or not. But then at least it starts with -- perhaps we leave D36 for a moment. It starts with D70, and then in an uninterrupted range up to and including D87. First, Mr. Re, are there any objections at all against --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There's no objection to any of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- the things that Colonel Crosland --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then D70 -- we will check for D36. But D70 up to and including D87 are admitted into evidence. Then we -- as far as Prosecution exhibits are concerned, we start with P70, and then I have an uninterrupted range up to P116. Are there any objections by any of the Defence teams on any of the documents in this range?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then P70 up to and including P116 are admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'll first make a correction to that. I said the range was uninterrupted. That is not correct, because on the list P99 does not appear. But there is a serious risk that we were confusing P -- let me just have a look. No. P99 was not in the range I just admitted into evidence. We'll have to have a look at what P99 exactly is, whether it was already admitted, which is a possibility. We'll check that, but at least that's not now subject of the Chamber's decision on admission. So, therefore, the range would then be from P70 up to P98 and including that, then restarting at P100 and up to and including P116. We'll further check P99 later on. Then today immediately admitted was P323, which was a map marked by Mr. Crosland; and the other map marked by Mr. Crosland is P324, which has not been admitted yet. May I take it that there's no objection against P324? That means that we'll still need to pay further attention to D36 and P99. I further draw your attention to the following. The Limaj transcript happen admitted into evidence; however, although the Chamber has heard that there were no objections against any of the exhibits used during that testimony, that being Exhibit P92 in the Limaj case, not in this case, and if that remains the same, that is, that there are no objections, then we will already decide, provisionally decide, to admit the 52 documents which we find under the P92 in Limaj. Madam Registrar will assign numbers to them and complete that list, and the reason why the admission is provisional is because the Chamber would like to look at these documents as well, whether they are suitable for admission. Because even if it's highly appreciated that the Defence does not object, the Chamber, of course, reserves its right to see whether these are documents that can be admitted. We'll do that the following way: They are admitted with the proviso that if the Chamber, in reviewing the matter, finds that there's any of these 52 documents, which still have to be assigned numbers to by Madam Registrar, would in the Chamber's view be inadmissible, we'll then inform the parties about it. So "provisional" means that they are admitted on the basis of there being no objections, but the Chamber already announces that it will review whether any correction is needed in the future. Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just on that a small logistical, administrative matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There is an overlap between some of the exhibits which you have admitted through the Defence and the Limaj DipTels. For example, D87 is 9229, D76 is 9233, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you have a comparison -- you don't have them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I've cross-checked some. I've noticed three. There are probably more which are from the Limaj which you've already admitted through the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the ruling is changed is that from these 52 documents attached to the Limaj transcript any document not yet admitted in this case will be admitted with the proviso that the Chamber will have an opportunity to review that. That is then on the record. And to the extent the parties are able to assist Madam Registrar in making a comparison between the 52 documents of Limaj and a list of exhibits we've got now, that would be appreciated. Mr. Crosland, I think we even managed without you, which is quite an achievement in this court, looking at what happened on the 19th, the 20th of April, and yesterday and today. Therefore, I'd like to thank you very much and wish you a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, are you ready to call your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just before Mr. Re --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- does, may I tidy up those two outstanding matters of exhibits that Your Honour had raised questions about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's D36 and P99, is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry. D70, which is tab 14, first of all, which was the document in respect of which during Mr. Re's re-examination, I circulated the official translation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- in hard copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: That will be, if it has not yet been, substituted for the draft translation which links to D70.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You would say that the official translation replaces the provisional translation until now attached to D70?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's uploaded. And, Madam Registrar, I take it that you will -- it's already done, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, very well. The other one was tab 17, D34, which was the document which when Your Honour looked at the original, there were two versions, one with some manuscript markings and another with a stamp, and yet a single translation which bore the stamp, but also seems to bear a translation of certain manuscript markings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The provisional solution agreed between the parties, if Your Honour is happy with it, is for D34 to remain the document which is currently the first of the two, and for the second of the two to be ascribed a separate exhibit number so that both documents are loaded into the system, they being different the one from the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And then for the parties to ensure that the translations of the two documents are linked and correlate. It may well be at the end of the day nothing whatever turns on the difference between the two, but to avoid that confusion and clarify that is the solution we propose. And if Your Honour's in agreement, we will have that dealt with outside court over the next 24 or 36 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's fine. Perhaps we already asked Madam Registrar to assign a number to the second version of that document, that document being the Pristina Corps command order dated the 28th of May, 1998.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be then Exhibit Number D88, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. The decisions I just gave on admission are always in line with what was said earlier about whether they were marked for identification, under seal or not. We'll have to review, Mr. Re, I take it the Limaj list, to see whether there are any -- whether there's any of these documents admitted under seal. All --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All the Limaj documents are admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: All the Limaj documents are under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'd forgotten when I explored whether there were any objections against P324; and when we found that there was not, I have not specifically said that P324 was admitted into evidence. Any further matter at this moment? Then, Mr. Re, are you ready to call your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. Our next witness is Ded Krasniqi. He requires no protective measures. Mr. Di Fazio will take that witness, and can I introduce, we have a new lawyer who arrived in the office several weeks ago, Ms. Rut Ley, who will be assisting Mr. Di Fazio. I notice Mr. Guy-Smith is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But I'll first say welcome to you, Ms. Ley, before I give an opportunity to Mr. Guy-Smith to raise whatever he wants to raise. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I also welcome you, Ms. Ley. I rise to ask the following question with regard to the next witness to be called, Mr. Krasniqi. We received late last night -- excuse me. We received at approximately 6.30 p.m., last night, Rule 68 information that indicated, among other things, that the next witness was convicted for a murder involving a dispute over cow pasturing as a result of a press release. We also received a series of newspaper articles that are in, I believe, Serbo-Croatian and some other documents. I have no way of knowing whether or not the newspaper articles are of any relevance and need investigation at this time because of the fact that they received them so late and they have not been translated. I have been informed by Mr. Di Fazio that he had an informal translation done of those documents, and I understand that to mean that the translator read them quickly. And based on whatever that translation was, he made a determination that they were Rule 68 and believed after sending them to us that his obligations were discharged in that regard. Apart from the difficulties that potentially may exist with regard to the late disclosure of this information, I rise to ask at this point: Is there any other Rule 68 information that the Office of the Prosecutor has with regard to this witness or the next witness? And this is especially in light of the representations previously made by the Office of the Prosecutor that they have a system in place whereby they have somebody who is reviewing the files for purposes of making sure that we get Rule 68 information, not only delivered to us but in a timely fashion so we can do something intelligent with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Mr. Di Fazio, may I take it -- or Mr. Re, may I take it that what was provided yesterday to the Defence has been received by the OTP recently? If these are newspaper articles, then at least we could start looking at when they were published.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I can't answer when this was received. I can put it in context. The first paragraph of the witness, or paragraph 3 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- say that he was imprisoned for 12 years. It's pretty obvious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What's obvious, Mr. Re -- let's go to the core. Do you know when you received that information. Is it known when these newspaper were published?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio can answer that better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I think they're quite old.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They're quite old. Okay. If they are contemporaneous to the imprisonment, to say it this way --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I might be of some assistance, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Apparently, the press release comes from 1982. It has an ERN number on it of some considerable age from my analysis of the ERN numbers as they exist in this case. The newspaper article I, have been led to believe, comes from 1995. It also has an older ERN number on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And were they or were they not disclosed any earlier, Mr. Re?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I can't answer that, but I can answer that it is an open-source document within the ERN range which is on the electronic disclosure suite and is searchable by the Defence. This came to our attention yesterday when we were doing some final searches for the witness and we disclosed some what is fairly obvious open-source material in relation to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. What exactly the importance of it being open-source material is still to be seen, but let's -- from your understanding, it's clear that the statement that has been provided to the Chamber starts with a rather long term of imprisonment, to say the least. Does this information, as far as you are aware of, give anything more than the type of offence or crime for which this was imposed and whether it was imposed and what court, or does it give any information beyond the scope of the criminal case in which this sentence was imposed? MR. DI FAZIO: They're just rudimentary newspaper articles that really don't go beyond the fact that it arose from a neighbourhood dispute over, as Mr. Guy-Smith mentioned, some dispute over the pasture of cows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is the -- yes, Mr. Troop.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps I can just invite the Prosecution to indicate in relation to one of the newspaper articles. The newspaper I'm referring to is one from, I believe, 1995. From our understanding, Mr. Krasniqi was released from prison in 1994. Because the newspaper is in Serbian and in Cyrillic, it is not possible for us even to get a basic understanding of the relevance of that article. As the Prosecution have the capacity and the ability to read this newspaper, and clearly they have some understanding of what that particular newspaper relates to, perhaps we could invite the Prosecution just to give an indication of what that particular newspaper means and how it may be relevant. MR. DI FAZIO: I can go no further than to tell you that I understand from having spoken briefly with an interpreter yesterday, that the newspaper articles --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How long is the newspaper article? MR. DI FAZIO: A page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A page. That's too much to read aloud. MR. DI FAZIO: I don't think there are any -- I think this is the one page, and I spoke to the interpreter yesterday. I gathered, from speaking -- the translator I should say. I gathered from speaking to them that it related to this incident. And as other material I had in English that related to the incident I had decided was Rule 68, I also decided to disclose this particular newspaper article. But what it says in detail, I don't know and I'm not in possession of a draft or official translation of the -- of what the newspaper article says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Is it -- of course, one of the issues that might become relevant in this context, Mr. Di Fazio, would be whether the victim or the relatives of the victim of that crime at the time, whether they play any role in the testimony to come. I remember that there was one additional observation about who was the enemy of the witness. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, of course -- I mean, if we're talking -- it's just something in the past about cows. That of course could gain some relevance in view of the testimony. MR. DI FAZIO: Well, it might, but I don't have any information to that effect. It might. I don't -- I don't know is the answer. I don't know. There's no names that I've seen in these -- in the English, brief English accounts that I've looked at that jump out and tell me that they are personalities or characters linked to this case. Now, for all I know, the Defence may have information to that effect, but the Prosecution doesn't, other than of course the involvement of the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you tell us how you came across these newspaper articles recently. I mean, in what context your attention was drawn to it. MR. DI FAZIO: I was reviewing -- I was reviewing materials for the purpose of isolating Rule 68 materials. I came across this material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And did you search by computer or -- MR. DI FAZIO: It was materials that was provided to me by others who had conducted a search. What parameters they used --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: -- what terms, definitions they used, how they conducted the search of the computer database, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: Having done that, they provided the materials to me to for me to review. I reviewed them and disclosed this material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that happened when? MR. DI FAZIO: Yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yesterday. Then the last question, but I take it that you have implicitly answered that question, whether there's any more Rule 68 material for this witness or the next witness to come, I would have expected you to have immediately disclosed such materials. Though -- but if you have any reason to believe there would be more Rule 68 material in relation to this witness or the next witness, I would like to hear from you. MR. DI FAZIO: I don't believe there is any more Rule 68 material relating to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But for the next witness. MR. DI FAZIO: But for the next witness, I can't speak to the next witness. Mr. Re is going to do that, but I haven't conducted any search in relation to the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps you pass that question to that member of your team who is going to deal with the next witness. MR. DI FAZIO: I would be grateful --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, it is Mr. Re. MR. DI FAZIO: It is Mr. Re, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Because I don't wish to take up any more time here, it might be appropriate for me to file a written explanation of the EDS system regarding general collections as well as to specific collections because the representations made here today are inaccurate. But I am happy to do that in writing, so the Court has a better understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The problem occurs efficiently often and is highlighted just today that I am raising that as a different issue, but I'm happy to make a written submission on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You're invited to do so and, of course, the Chamber will have a look at it. Mr. Re -- Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: May I have one sentence for the record. Researches during the course of the morning have revealed that this material was used by the Prosecution in the prosecution of Slobodan Milosevic to cross-examine -- to cross-examine a witness called by Mr. Milosevic. That appears to be its genesis. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, might I rectify that. I understand, and my case manager hopefully will correct me, perhaps if he could look into this while --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I suggest the following. I suggest that we have an early break and that we do not start either alleging or rectifying or doing anything else unless we have verified the information we have received. I also suggest to the parties that if we have an early break, that at least copies of the originals are available to everyone, and that we use our resources to the best of your abilities to get as good as we can an impression of what these newspaper articles tell us. So that we have a -- well, I was about to say a proper basis for further discussion, but as a matter of fact I would like to say a proper basis for not having too many further discussions on the matter because we know better what we are talking about. Of course, it's usually not that the Chamber starts examining material which has not been produced in this courtroom. But under the present circumstances and in view of the fact that the Chamber might be called upon to rule anyhow on whether there's a violation of any disclosure obligation here, I take it that the parties would not mind that if the Chamber would do the same as it invites the parties to do. Then the Chamber would like to be provided with a hard copy of the newspaper articles, and we'll find each other in our rush whether to see to get the assistants to understand what they say. Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: How can we -- yes, we can do that. And what I might try and do during the break, if that's okay, try at least to get a summary printed, typed out by one of our interpreters of the Serb Cyrillic article. Secondly, how can we get the other material to you, to the Trial Chamber, through the registry officer during the break? I assume you want it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, I suggest that you give it to the Legal Officer and he will provide it to us. MR. DI FAZIO: Fine. We'll do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I suggest we have a break now and after the break, if possible, we would like to start with the examination of the witness, unless there are compelling reasons not to do so. We'll have a break until 25 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that a summary has been distributed; everyone is granted 45 seconds to read it. Having read it and on the basis of the information the Chamber received, it seems that the 1995 newspaper article primarily looks back at the event in 1982, that it describes in some more detail on what happened at the time, and that it places the incident in a situation of ethnic -- at least, among others, as in a context of ethnic conflict, that it describes the difficulties to live later on. From what the Chamber understood, none of the names mentioned here are -- do appear anywhere in the witness statement. There's only one little matter which perhaps might need some attention; that is, that in the correction the witness gave on his earlier statement, someone is described as being the enemy of the son. If it would be the son of an enemy, that might have considerably changed the matter, but that's not at least what the Chamber has read. If any of the parties would consider the present newspaper article, as we had access to, whether that would be a compelling reason not to start the testimony of the witness, I'd like to hear it, otherwise -- I see nodding no, Mr. Emmerson, no. Then, Mr. Di Fazio, are you ready to call your next witness? MR. DI FAZIO: I am. I am. And if I might just -- it will take me a minute, if Your Honours please. I just want to put some matters into perspective.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, I do understand that was some miscommunication as to what time we would start again. It's nice to have this written summary. I don't know. The Chamber doesn't find much new in there from what it already understood, and I wouldn't summarize it not on the basis of the written summary. Let's get started, unless there's really a compelling reason not to do that and if there's any need at a later stage to put matters into context, then -- MR. DI FAZIO: Just this. I just disclosed a document now, now, to the Defence. If the Defence turn the page, they just turn the page and look at 3888, they will see the relevant part of this document. It refers to a 43-year-old Serb, Miodrag Saric. That's the relevant part. That was just disclosed now. It was not disclosed yesterday because due to a mistake, and it was a clerical error, we looked at in fact the document, but our information was that it had been disclosed in the past in a previous batch. That information was incorrect. I've just now disclosed it. I am from the Prosecution's point of view, this article is inconsequential to the nth agree, in the Prosecution's view. However, if the Defence wants to raise anything, now is the time. They can read it. It should take, I would say, all of eight seconds to read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Eight seconds are over, but I don't know whether -- you could ask for more.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No. I've read it earlier on and I've seen what it says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No further, then we will -- MR. DI FAZIO: I'm ready to proceed, and if Your Honours please, I call Ded Krasniqi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Usher, could you please escort Mr. Krasniqi into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I, meanwhile, take the opportunity to inform the parties that the Chamber, for administrative reasons, has decided that any exhibit used during the testimony of Witness 8, whatever the fate of that may be in the future, shall be assigned exhibit numbers in order not to lose them from our lists. So, therefore, it's just for administrative purposes and does not anticipate in whatever way on future events in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I take it that Your Honour intends that indication to apply not just to exhibits used, but to exhibits that were to be used; in other words, to the material that was in the file for cross-examination or merely to those which were in fact --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think, as a matter of fact, for those, in fact, used because the others -- but we'll have to check that on the list. Yes. Usually, we do not assign numbers to documents where they have not been used in any way or not. And your intent to use that, if that ever turns into reality, then, of course, immediately numbers will be assigned.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The reason I'm hesitating is because Madam Registrar very kindly raised with me the index to the cross-examination bundle, and I think may have raised that after the conversation with me with the Trial Chamber. Now, there are, in fact, two items that were produced during the testimony as I recall it. One is the video which has been marked for identification but not yet admitted, and the other was a very late-produced statement that came from the Prosecution at the very end, which I think has not been marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: All of the documents in the cross-examination bundle, as far as I recall it, we didn't get to the point where they had, in fact, been used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will check that, but most important is that any document that was used in court appears on our list as --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- marked for identification so that we don't lose them out of sight.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, I think this will be of sufficient guidance to you, as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I could also use our time to read a decision, that is a decision on the application for issuance of a subpoena for the person with Prosecution Witness Number 50. The Chamber finds that the test for issuance of a subpoena for this witness has not been met. In particular, the Chamber considers that the Prosecution has failed to demonstrate in paragraph 5 of its application that the witness is likely to provide information that will materially assist the Prosecution's case. The Chamber has read the 65 ter summary of the expected testimony of the witness and has as well considered the 65 ter summaries of other witnesses expected to testify on the same counts. Our conclusion is that the expected testimony of the witness in question is purely corroborative and largely hearsay and does not cover any critical elements of the allegations in the indictment that are not already covered through apparently better evidence of other witnesses. The Chamber emphasises that the application is denied without prejudice to the Prosecution; in other words, the Prosecution is entitled, if it wishes, to submit another application for subpoena of this witness, but only if it is able to make a significantly stronger case for calling this witness. This concludes the Chamber's decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Krasniqi. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. May I invite you to make that declaration, of which the text is now handed out to you by Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, please be seated. Mr. Krasniqi, you'll first be examined by Mr. Di Fazio, who's counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Di Fazio, you may proceed. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, what ethnicity are you?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. And in 1998, I'd like you to try and give the Trial Chamber an idea of your family, your family members in 1998. So tell us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I first ask you, is there any objection against leading on these personal matters?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: None whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's as far as ethnicity, dates of birth, composition of the family, et cetera. Mr. Di Fazio, so perhaps you could speed that up. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: In 1998, you had how many-- MR. DI FAZIO: To tell you the truth, if Your Honours please, I don't actually know the answer to this so I'd like to ask the witness directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: How many sons did you have in 1998, early 1998?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I had three.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Right. And you also had a daughter, I believe?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI
utterances.text: And one daughter, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And you used to live in the city of Peje or Pec, the town of Peje or Pec?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Was one of your son's Pal Krasniqi?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. In 1998, did your son decide to join the KLA?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Can you recall about what time of the year that was?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI
utterances.text: It was in 1998, July the 10th.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Right. Now, is that the date that he went off to join the KLA?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Had you and he discussed his joining the KLA before that?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So you were aware on the 10th of July, 1998, of his plans?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know a gentleman or did you know in 1998 a gentleman named Mahir Dema?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was he a friend of your son's?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did he have any plans in 1998 to join the KLA?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. He told me about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Who told you about Mr. Mahir Dema's plans, your son; or did Mahir Dema himself tell you of Mahir Dema's plans to join the KLA?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Mahir Dema and my son, both of them told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well. Now, you said that on the 10th of July, 1998, they went off to join the KLA. Am I correct in my understanding?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What I would like to know is: Were you made aware of where exactly they were going in order to carry out this plan of joining the KLA?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. They did tell me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And what did they tell you?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI
utterances.text: They told me that they would be going to Jablanica, but they had to go to Klina first to get my wife and bring her there and then go to Jablanica. And on the way, they were apprehended at the Krusha e Madhe check-point, police check-point. They were beaten up there and taken to Klina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Just pause there. I want you to -- please tell me if my understanding of your evidence is correct. Mahir Dema and your son told you that they were going to pick up your wife from Klina and return with her to your home in Peje or Pec. Do I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. And do I understand you correctly that the plan was: Having done that, that those two young men would then go to Jablanica to join the KLA? Do I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you started to mention that something happened to them at a police check-point. I want you first to tell the Trial Chamber how you know what happened to them at the -- at the check-point, how you have this information, how you are in a position to be able to tell us.

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI
utterances.text: When they went to Klina, they did not return until the morning. At 6.00 in the morning, they called me on the telephone from Klina, and I asked him, "My son, Where are you?" He told me that the police had beaten them up and they were feeling very weak, and if I could go and help them. I said, "I can't come and help you because the police are looking for me as well." I asked him, "Where are you?" And he said, "I am at the church." I could hear a door opening and closing, and I did not believe my son, whether he was at the church or at the police station. And I thought maybe the police had forced him to call me, but he swore to me that he was at the church. But still, I did not believe him. I didn't know in whose hands he was. And I told my son, "You know, my son, we have discussed something together. Do you remember?" And he said, "Yes." And I told him then, "Please, go to where we discussed before and try not to fall in the hands of the friend you know." And when he arrived there, he had to get some weapons, at least get a weapon for me as well, and come and take me in Peje. I didn't know where to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI
utterances.text: And that was the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Thank you for recounting that. I just want to be clear about one thing. You said that you told your son something and that your son and you had discussed something together, and you asked him to remember this during the telephone conversation. What topic were you referring to when you said that to your son? What was it that you had discussed and what were you urging him to do?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I was still scared that he was in the hands of the Serbs, so I didn't want to mention the KLA. That's why I told him, "Go to where we discussed before," but the idea was for them to go and join the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So in your mind when you told him to go where you had discussed, you were referring to Jablanica. Do I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, did you see this young man, Mahir Dema, again?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI
utterances.text: After the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when -- can you tell us when that was. Now, was it in 1998 that you saw him, or maybe the next year? Can you be a little bit more precise, please.

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI
utterances.text: After the liberation, after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know how many months after you had telephone conversation that you've just told us about that you next saw Mahir Dema?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI
utterances.text: From that moment on, I did not see my son anymore. But after the war, I saw Mahir Dema in Peje and I asked him whether he knew anything about my son, but he was scared. And I asked him, "Why are you afraid?" He said, "Please, don't look for him. Nobody will dare to say anything about it. Let things settle down first." And he said, "I have a friend in Pristina and we will try to find him." That was the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do you have -- do you know if Mahir Dema ever went to hospital?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI
utterances.text: He was in the military hospital in Jablanica; before that, he was in Peje, where he had an operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did he have the operation before this episode that you're talking about when your son went --

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. I'm not interested then in that. Did Mahir Dema ever talk to you about when he last saw your son?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI
utterances.text: He told me that they went to Jablanica, and Mahir was beaten up more severely -- had been beaten up more severely than my son.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI
utterances.text: They had asked him -- the police had asked him, "Why have you come to Klina?"

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Now, just to be absolutely clear about this, this beating that Mahir and your son also had suffered, was that at the hands of Serb police?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI
utterances.text: The Serb police in Klina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Thank you. Now continue. I was asking you about Mahir Dema and whether he ever spoke to you about when he last saw your son. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI
utterances.text: He told me about the time when they had gone together to Jablanica, and our army had taken Mahir to the hospital for him to be cured. And my son had joined his companions, his comrades. A couple of days later my son had gone to visit him at the hospital, and they greeted each other and that was the last time he saw my son. Mahir Dema was sent to Istok, former Istok now called Burim, and then he went to Montenegro to get a cure because he was very ill. That's what he told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, I just want to ask you this: From what Mahir Dema told you, do you have any idea how long after these two young men set off to go and join the KLA in Jablanica that this hospital visit occurred. About how long after -- after they set off together to join the KLA did Mahir see your son in hospital? Did you -- do you have any information about that from Mahir?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. He told me about five days later, and after that they did not meet again. This is what Mahir told me because I did not hear anything from my son.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. We all understand that you're talking now about what Mahir told you, and I'd just like to move on to another topic. But just before I do, I want us to be absolutely sure so the Trial Judges can understand what you're saying. You understood -- you tell me if this is correct. You understood that the two young men had set off for Jablanica on July 10th --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The 10th, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: -- July 10, July 10, 1998, and along the way they were beaten up by Serb police, and about five days later Mahir saw your son in hospital. Now, is my understanding correct?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And as far as you're aware from what Mahir told you, was that the last time Mahir saw him as well?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I don't -- perhaps it's just me who is confused by the language "in hospital." I know that Mahir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, that could be understood in two different ways. We have read the statement of the witness. We have heard his testimony. The two last questions were superfluous, anyhow. And, of course, while in hospital, it is clear that Mahir was the one who was the patient and the other one was visiting. That is so clear from -- so, therefore, yes, the language was unclear; but in the context, it was perfectly clear and I wonder how we could have understood the testimony in any other way as you summarized it. So, therefore, the summary was not necessary. Please proceed. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you start to make attempts to locate your son?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. I made several attempts. First of all, I went to Jablanica, and from there I couldn't learn anything. So I went to Klina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Can I just interrupt you there. I'd like to ask you about Jablanica first. About how long after July 10, 1998, would you say that you went to Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI
utterances.text: It was after the war; before that, I couldn't go.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So was it a matter of months?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI
utterances.text: It was late autumn, September, October.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Of the same year that your son went off to join the KLA?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No, no. Before the war ended, I could not go to look for my son.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Who did you speak with at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, let's try to clarify this. Is there any common understanding of the parties on when the war was over? MR. DI FAZIO: I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there was any war. MR. DI FAZIO: Well, the important thing is for this witness's understanding, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. You ask him same year? He said: No, no, no, before the war ended. And then it seems that you move on to your next question, so the Chamber still doesn't know when he went. Would that be -- but let's perhaps ask the witness ourselves. You said: "After the war was over." How long it took until the war was over after your son had left on the 10th of July? Mr. Krasniqi, could you please answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it was after the war. One or two months after the war, things settled down a little bit, and I asked -- started to ask people if they had seen my son.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you said: "After the war." When did the war stop in view of you? Was that in that same summer of 1998? Was it in the winter to follow? Was it in the summer after that? Could you please tell us when you considered the war was over.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was in the year 2000, and that's when I started to look for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is, therefore, two years after your son had left; is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Why did you wait for two years?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I didn't know where to go and look for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Very well. You went to Jablanica. Now, who -- do you know any individual, the names of any individuals that you spoke with at Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What was the name of the person or persons that you spoke with at Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI
utterances.text: It was Hamez Ukshini from Jablanica. I spoke with him mostly, but there was another person, Abdul Zeneli, but he couldn't give me any information.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And who precisely was Hamez Ukshini?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I knew him from before. I also knew his father, and that's why I went to him, to ask him for any information that he might have, but he didn't say anything. He didn't give me any information. He said that this name has not existed in Jablanica. It was not here; this name I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did he know of other names that he -- that had existed at Jablanica? Did he know of other names?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. He had other names because he said, "I will look in a notebook." And that's when he told me that this name is not registered here. "He was never here."

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. That's what I wanted to know. When you were with him, was he looking at some document or something like that to consult names, from what you could see? That's what I would like to know.

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What was the notebook that he had? Did you -- did that have any names in it?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI
utterances.text: He only spoke to me just orally.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you see him look at a notebook while you spoke to him?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI
utterances.text: He did not have any notebook in front of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did he say that he would look in a notebook, and that's all you know?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Now, this gentleman, Mr. Hamez Ukshini, was he a member of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do you know if he held any position within the KLA, whether he was an official or did something specific in the KLA?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, he had.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Can you give us details. What was his job? What was his position?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI
utterances.text: As he told me in his house, he said, "I've been here involved with the clinic, with the food, and with the comings and goings from our army. And the name of your son is not anywhere on the lists here," and that was the last time that I saw him or spoke to him. I've never seen him afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Did you continue in your efforts to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one question to have it clarified. When he was talking about the list, did he explain to you what kind of list these were? Was this a list of KLA members? Was this a list of patients? Was this a list of villagers? Could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He had the list of the members of the KLA who came in and went out to different directions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Following this episode, did you make further attempts to get information about your son?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What was the next step that you took?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I knew someone, another commander of the KLA. I tried to reach him, but it was very difficult. The policeman helped me to get in touch with him, and I met him in Klina. I waited for him to come out of a hotel, and the policeman said, "Wait, he's coming." So I went together with him; we greeted each other. I went -- we went up to his office on the second floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I just ask you to pause there. You said that you knew someone, another commander of the KLA. What's the name of this gentleman?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI
utterances.text: He is called Alush Agushi, alias Pipi.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: How long had you known Alush Agushi, alias Pipi?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI
utterances.text: When I came out of prison in 1994, in June, he came to see me in my home, together with the brother of my wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. So you had known this man for a number of years, had you?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you know him before 1994?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Had you seen him since you met him in 1994 when he came together with the brother of your wife?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No. No, I had never seen him before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You met him with the brother of your wife. After you met him with the brother of your wife, after that, did you ever see him again, apart from this incident in Klina; in other words, in between?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: When you saw him in Klina on this -- in this inquiry that you were making about your son, did you have any trouble recognising him or identifying him? Did you know who he was?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I know him, because we had met during the funerals of the martyrs. We went to pay tribute to those people. We saw each other, but never had a chance to talk.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. So you met him in 1994, once, when he came to your house with your wife's brother, you saw him at funerals and you saw him again on this occasion in Klina. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, tell us, how did matters develop with Mr. Agushi? What did he tell you, and what did you tell him?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI
utterances.text: When we went to the second floor, we sat down and started talking. I asked him whether he knew who I was, and he said, "No." I put on a smile and said, "You remember when you came to visit me in 1994 when I came out of prison," and then he remembered. I told him that I was there looking for my son because I've heard from his fellow soldiers that he was in Jablanica with them. He said, "Wait a moment," and then he went out to another office and took a sheet and started taking notes. I was explaining him details, what I knew, and he told me that, In two weeks' time, I will let you know." And I told him, "One month will do." That's where the conversation ended. I returned home. I waited for a long time, but no reply came. I tried again to contact him, but some friends of mine told me that he has been transferred to Pristina. I was on my own at home, and it was very difficult to travel to Pristina at that time. I went there. They showed me to where the barracks of our army was. There at the entrance, there were some soldiers. I reported. I gave them my name and family name, and they asked me, "What do you want?" I told them, "I want to meet the commander." I gave them my details. I also mentioned them this pseudonym of Ramush Haradinaj, as well as that of Alush Agushi, Pipi. They told me, "You have to wait because they are in a meeting." I waited for a pretty long time. I had no watch on me, but I noticed that it was very late and that the guards -- the guards changed, because they stayed there for several hours and then they changed. And I had to tell the new guards again from the start what I was waiting for. One of them ran into a building nearby and asked me to wait. I waited for quite a while. He came back to say, "You've got to go back to your home and never come back again because no commander is here". But I told him I was told that they are in a meeting. They said, "Go, go. Go back home." And I didn't ask for him, but when I have been to the funerals of the nephews of Ramush Haradinaj -- rather, the funerals of my nephews and Ramush Haradinaj was there, but we didn't greet each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: The result is, I gather from your evidence, that you didn't ever get any information from your trip to Pristina and the barracks, is that correct, the information about your son?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do you know the village of Bardosan?

utterances.speaker: DED KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, as you know, the Chamber is provided with the witness statements and also with anything that appears new. May I ask your attention, the witness statement, paragraph 15, fourth line contains information which seems not to be without relevance. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It has not appeared in the testimony until now, and it seems that you're moving to your next subject. Therefore, I wonder either during proofing the situation as changed with the Chamber being informed or whether you would still expect the witness to give this testimony, which might again assist the Chamber in better understanding the totality of the testimony of this witness. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you come to that at a later stage, then of course it's fine, but it looked as if you're moving to the next subject. MR. DI FAZIO: In, Your Honours. Firstly, there's nothing in proofing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: The notes you've got represents everything I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: He didn't mentioned that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm happy for him to lead. I'm happy for Mr. Di Fazio to lead. MR. DI FAZIO: No, I'm will lead him. I am not trying to conceal it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no. You were moving on to Bardosan; whereas, I would expect another person who will -- MR. DI FAZIO: No. I will do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, when you went to Klina and the police station and you met with this gentleman, Alush Agushi, also known as Pipi, and he went and got his papers and took down details about your son and said that he'd get back to you, did he mention anything about your son having been with him until the Serb offensive in September? Was there any mention made of that by Mr. Pipi -- sorry, Mr. Agushi?

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: Can I just interrupt?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Perhaps first hear the answer of the witness, unless there's any objection against the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: It relates to the question. Mr. Di Fazio isn't reading or isn't using the same phrasing as is used in the witness statement. If he is going to lead, may I ask that he use the accurate wording.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me --

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: There's a difference. He said "the Serb offensive," when in fact the statement said "the first offensive." MR. DI FAZIO: The Serb offensive in September 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I think it -- MR. DI FAZIO: I'm sorry, "the first offensive of 1998."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's now try to get it clear for the witness. Did Mr. Agushi tell you anything about your son being with him until an offensive in September?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. He told me the same day that he was taking notes, he said that, "He was with us. We were surrounded by the Serbian army and I told my soldiers to go in whatever direction they thought it proper."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As he said "with us," did he specify for how long?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Up until the end of September he told me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Di Fazio. Well, as a matter of fact, I'm looking at the clock. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm out of time I think. I've got that one minor topic and that will be the end of it tomorrow, for the examination-in-chief, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand. Mr. Krasniqi, we have to finish for the day. I'd like to see you back tomorrow morning, the 25th, in another courtroom, in Courtroom I. And I want to instruct you that you should not speak with anyone about your testimony, whether it be the testimony you gave today or the testimony still to be given tomorrow. Is that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Madam Usher, could you please escort Mr. Krasniqi out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, is it correct that we have not yet received a statement for the next witness? Is that correct? MR. DI FAZIO: Mr. Re will be making that -- attending to that matter, but I can just inquire of my case manager and find out, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if not, then we'd like to receive it as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: I believe it was sent this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This morning, then I might have missed it. MR. DI FAZIO: This morning. You should have it. If our information is correct, a simple phone call to our case manager will clarify the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then we stand adjourned to tomorrow morning, 9.00, Courtroom I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 25th day of May, 2007, at 9.00 a.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.46 p.m.,
